sn51.1:1.1: _Iddhi_ (Sanskrit _ṛddhi_) conveys the root sense “increase, success”. In the Atharva Veda we find _samṛddhi_ and _vyṛddhi_  in the sense “prosperity” and “misfortune” (eg. 10.2.10). As “success, completion” (of the sacrifice) we find _ṛddhi_ at Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.6.9.11. As far as I know, the Buddhist texts are where we first find _iddhi_ in the sense of “psychic power” ([sn51.10:3.2](), [sn51.11:5.1]()). This sense is not attested in Sanskrit texts until later, where we find eight such powers mentioned (Bhāgavata Purāṇa 3.20.53, 9.21.12). This number is also found in Jain texts, which list various kinds of _ṛddhi_ or _labdhi_ (eg. Ṭhāṇaṅga 5.168, Bhagavatisūtra 8.139). Perhaps this idea was first popularized among the _śramaṇa_ schools such as Buddhism and Jainism. All these religions, however, aim at liberation from suffering, and do not regard the attainment of psychic powers as an end in itself. It seems likely that the interest in such abilities was drawn from the broader ascetic culture, where to this day we find a fascination with such powers. In the Indian context, it is important to avoid such terms as “supernatural”, as such phenomena, though extraordinary, are always considered as well within the realm of the natural. They do not arise from the intervention of God or any other metaphysical means, but rather from the development and amplification of abilities latent in all beings. This teaching framework, accordingly, focuses on those things that form the *bases* (_pāda_) of psychic power, and the powers themselves are mere adornments to the path, whose true purpose is to lead “from the near shore to the far shore”.
